title: India Pushes 'One Nation, One Licence' Reforms to Let Doctors Practice Across States
excerpt: The National Medical Commission's centralized register and new draft amendments aim to end the state-by-state licensing maze that has long restricted physician mobility in India.
body:
• India's National Medical Register (NMR) now offers doctors a single Unique Identification Number (UID) that can be used to apply for licences across states, replacing the fragmented state-by-state system.
  • Draft amendments published in April 2026 allow Armed Forces Medical Services (AFMS) doctors to register with one State Medical Council and practice nationwide during their service.
  • The Centre has proposed NMR-based interstate practice to states like Kerala under its 'Compliance Reduction and Deregulation' initiative, recommending that doctors registered anywhere be allowed to practice without fresh registration.
  • NITI Aayog is separately pushing regulatory reforms for professional services, including licence portability for healthcare workers, to boost India's services exports.

A Unified Medical Register Takes Shape

For decades, Indian doctors have navigated a fragmented licensing system that requires separate registrations with each State Medical Council where they wish to practice. A physician registered in Maharashtra who wants to treat patients in Karnataka must obtain a fresh registration — often involving paperwork, fees, and an NOC from the originating state.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has been working to dismantle this system through the National Medical Register, a centralized digital platform launched in August 2025 by Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda. The NMR assigns each doctor a lifelong Unique Identification Number and consolidates records previously scattered across state registers. Data for approximately 14 lakh (1.4 million) doctors already registered in the Indian Medical Register is being migrated to the new system.

"The initiative of creating 'one nation one registration platform' for doctors is also aimed at eliminating duplication and red-tapism," Dr. Yogender Malik, Member of the Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) at NMC, said when the system was announced.

Armed Forces Doctors Get Nationwide Practice Rights

In April 2026, the NMC published draft amendments to the "Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations, 2023" specifically addressing military doctors. Under the proposed rules, physicians commissioned in the Armed Forces Medical Services (AFMS) would register with one State Medical Council of their choice and be authorized to practice across all states and Union Territories for the duration of their service.

"Doctors can be stopped from performing even life-saving procedures across NCR due to lack of local registration. These are pointless barriers."

— Dr. (Maj) Rajesh Bhardwaj, Consultant ENT, MedFirst ENT Centre

The amendment also ensures that AFMS doctors' licences will not lapse due to delayed renewal submissions, and any additional qualifications registered during service will be recognized nationwide. The NMC invited public comments on the draft through May 7, 2026.

Centre Pushes States Toward Interstate Practice

Beyond the military carve-out, the central government has begun pushing states to adopt broader licence portability. Under Phase II of its 'Compliance Reduction and Deregulation' initiative, the Centre proposed to the Kerala government that healthcare professionals registered with any state council or listed in the NMR should be allowed to practice in Kerala without applying again or seeking prior approval.

The proposal would work through self-certification, eliminating the current requirement for NOCs from a practitioner's previous state. Kerala's existing framework under the Kerala State Medical Practitioners Act, 2021 requires fresh registration for out-of-state doctors, nurses, and paramedical staff.

"The proposal to make registration in one state valid in another can help address the shortage of doctors, particularly in rural and border districts."

— Jobin Joseph, General Secretary, Kerala Government Medical Officers' Association

Implementation would require legislative changes at the state level, making the timeline uncertain. But the proposal signals a clear federal push toward treating medical registration as a national credential rather than a state-specific one.

Regulatory Reforms for Services Exports

Running parallel to the domestic licensing overhaul, NITI Aayog has been advocating broader regulatory reforms for India's professional services sector. The think tank's Trade Watch publications have called for interstate licence portability across healthcare and other professions, framing it as essential to India's ambition to boost services exports.

NITI Aayog has recommended that India negotiate mutual recognition agreements for professional qualifications — including healthcare — as part of trade deals with countries like the United States. The proposals also call for simplified licensing procedures and better data governance to help Indian firms compete globally.

What Comes Next

The transition from a state-based licensing regime to a national system will not happen overnight. While the NMR infrastructure is operational, the key question is whether states will voluntarily adopt the Centre's recommendations or whether legislative mandates will be needed. The AFMS amendments, once finalized, will serve as a precedent for broader reforms. Meanwhile, the NMR portal continues onboarding doctors and state councils onto a unified digital platform, building the technical backbone for what could eventually become true interstate licence portability for India's medical workforce.
nri_angle: Regulatory reforms could improve healthcare access for diaspora members visiting India and simplify credentialing for Indian-trained doctors seeking to practice across states.
author: Diaspora Desk
